entities.summary: Lugaid Íardonn, son of Énna Derg, was, according to medieval Irish legend and historical tradition, a High King of Ireland. His epithet, Old Irish for "dark brown", came from the colour of his hair. He succeeded his father, who had died of plague, to the throne, and ruled for nine years before he was killed at Ráth Clochair by Sírlám, son of Finn mac Blatha. The Lebor Gabála Érenn synchronises his reign with that of Artaxerxes I of Persia. The chronology of Geoffrey Keating's Foras Feasa ar Éirinn dates his reign to 658–649 BC, that of the Annals of the Four Masters to 881–872 BC.

entities.name: Lugaid Íardonn
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lugaid Íardonn (Old Irish: 'dark-brown Lugaid'), son of Énna Derg, was, according to medieval Irish legend and historical tradition, a High King of Ireland. His epithet came from the colour of his hair. He succeeded his father, who had died of plague, to the throne, and ruled for nine years before he was killed in battle.

Lugaid appears in the Lebor Gabála Érenn (Book of Invasions) and the Annals of the Four Masters as part of the mythologized prehistoric king-lists of Ireland. His reign is placed in the pre-Christian era, making him part of the semi-legendary sequence of High Kings that medieval Irish scholars used to construct a continuous regal history from the biblical Flood to the Christian period.

His historical verifiability is uncertain — the earliest High King-lists are largely mythological constructions assembled by monastic scholars in the 8th–10th centuries to provide Ireland with an ancient royal pedigree comparable to those of biblical and classical civilizations. Nonetheless, Lugaid Íardonn represents the medieval Irish tradition of kingship ideology: the king as sacred guardian of the land's fertility, whose personal character (including the color of his hair) was understood to manifest the health of the realm. His name appears in genealogical texts connecting later dynasties to the mythological past.
